subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Uday, since you asked about my blushing: it's the worst in assembly. Last term, the teacher asked me to read the morning thought. As soon as I walked to the microphone my face went hot, and I was sure that the whole hall was staring at my red cheeks. My heart was banging. What helped was small things. I breathed out slowly, longer than I breathed in. I looked at the page and at the back wall instead of watching myself in my head. And I reminded myself that most people are thinking about their own morning, not my face. I still turned red, and I read all the same. I'm Pallavi, by the way. Afterwards nobody said a word about it.

qa.q: Where is the blushing the worst for Pallavi?
qa.a: It is the worst in assembly.

qa.q: What was Pallavi afraid of at the microphone?
qa.a: Pallavi was afraid the whole hall was staring at those red cheeks, which fed the anxiety and the banging heart.

qa.q: What steps helped Pallavi while blushing?
qa.a: Pallavi breathed out slowly, looked at the page and the back wall, and remembered that most people were thinking about their own morning.

qa.q: How might the students in the hall have seen Pallavi?
qa.a: Most were probably busy with their own thoughts, so they likely didn't notice the blush as much as Pallavi feared.

grounding: A teen who blushes easily fears being noticed, and slow breathing, focusing outward and remembering most people don't notice help.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Payal got asked a question in biology, and I was sitting right behind her. She went red from her collar up to her ears. I saw her put down her pen and take one long breath out, then another. She looked at the diagram on the board rather than at anyone, and I heard her say, "Could you repeat the question, Miss?" Her voice was small but steady. She answered correctly. Afterwards she pressed the back of her hand to her cheek and gave a short laugh. I can't tell if she was frightened, or just hot, or embarrassed. She seemed to calm down after a bit. Nobody around us even glanced at her. - Indu

qa.q: What did Payal ask the teacher after she was called on?
qa.a: She asked the teacher to repeat the question.

qa.q: What might Payal have been feeling when she blushed?
qa.a: She was probably anxious about being looked at, shown by the long breaths and looking at the board, though Indu admits it could also have been heat or embarrassment.

qa.q: What helped Payal steady herself?
qa.a: Slow breaths and focusing on the diagram instead of the faces around her.

qa.q: How did the other students seem to see Payal's blush?
qa.a: Indu notes that nobody around them even glanced at her, which fits the idea that most people don't notice as much as the blusher fears.

grounding: A teen who blushes easily fears being noticed, and slow breathing and focusing outward help.

passage:
Monday: When the teacher called on Uday to read, his face went bright red, ears and neck too. He could feel it burning. He was sure the whole class was staring. He stumbled through two lines and sat down.
Wednesday: His friend Aditi noticed him pulling his collar up. At break she said, "When I get nervous, I breathe out slowly, longer than I breathe in. It calms the heat down." She also said, "Honestly? When you read, most people are looking at their books, not you."
Uday tried the breathing that night in front of the mirror. In for four, out for six.
Friday: His presentation on volcanoes. He felt the heat start. He breathed out slowly. He focused on the diagram, on the words, on explaining lava to the back row. He still went pink.
Afterwards, Aditi said, "Did you know you blushed?"
"Did everyone see?"
"I only noticed because I was looking for it."

qa.q: What was Uday's presentation about?
qa.a: Volcanoes.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when his face went red on Monday?
qa.a: Uday felt anxious and afraid of being noticed, sure the whole class was staring at his blushing.

qa.q: Which strategies helped Uday on Friday?
qa.a: Slow breathing with a longer out-breath, focusing outward on the diagram and audience, and remembering that most people don't notice.

qa.q: How did Aditi see Uday's blushing?
qa.a: Aditi barely noticed it and only saw it because she was looking, which shows others notice less than Uday feared.

grounding: The three beats show a teenager who blushes easily reducing the distress through slow breathing, outward focus and remembering most people don't notice.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Gautam, you've gone red again, haven't you? Come here. Your Hrithik Mama was worse, I promise.
At fifteen I blushed at everything. Ordering tea. Answering roll call. Once a girl just asked me the time and I turned the colour of a tomato. The more I thought "don't go red," the redder I went.
I started skipping class presentations. I pretended to be sick on sports day.
Then my cricket coach, Mr Batra, pulled me aside. He'd noticed. He said, "Hrithik, when you're batting, where do you look?"
"At the ball."
"Not at the crowd?"
"No."
"Then when you talk, look at the ball. The words. The person. Not at your own face. And breathe out slowly, like before a big shot."
I tried it. Still went red sometimes. But I stopped hiding. And, Gautam, most people never noticed. They were busy worrying about themselves.

qa.q: Who pulled Hrithik aside?
qa.a: His cricket coach, Mr Batra.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling at fifteen when he blushed?
qa.a: He felt anxious and embarrassed, afraid of being noticed, which made him skip presentations and sports day.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Hrithik Mama's story?
qa.a: Mr Batra's advice to focus outward, like watching the ball, and breathe out slowly, which helped Hrithik stop hiding.

qa.q: How did other people see Hrithik's blushing?
qa.a: Most never noticed, because they were busy worrying about themselves.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teenager's blushing and social anxiety eased by slow breathing, focusing outward and realising most people don't notice.

passage:
Lokesh had been chosen to read the morning announcements over the school PA, and on his first day the principal decided to sit in the office right next to the mic. Then the mic started crackling.
Lokesh felt the heat rise from his neck to his forehead. His hands were damp. He was sure the principal was staring at his red face.
His friend Akash, who ran the sound board, leaned over and whispered, "Breathe out. Long. Then just read the words, like you're reading to me."
Lokesh breathed out slowly. He looked only at the paper. Sports day timing. Library books due. Lost water bottle, blue, with a sticker.
His voice wobbled on the first line and steadied by the third.
When he finished, the principal just said, "Clear. Thank you," and went back to her files.
"Did she see me go red?" Lokesh whispered.
Akash shrugged. "She was reading her emails."

qa.q: What colour was the lost water bottle?
qa.a: Blue, with a sticker.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling as the mic crackled?
qa.a: Lokesh felt anxious and afraid of being noticed, his face going hot and hands damp.

qa.q: What did Akash suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Breathing out slowly and focusing only on the words, which moved Lokesh's attention outward and steadied his voice.

qa.q: How did the principal see Lokesh's announcement?
qa.a: She seemed to notice only that it was clear, since she was reading her emails, not watching his face.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager who blushes easily managing the fear of being noticed through slow breathing and outward focus under pressure.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Trisha knew the exact moment it would happen. Mrs Sen would say, "Trisha, your answer?" and heat would climb her neck like a tide, and she would be sure the whole Kolkata classroom could see it. Last week she had whispered "I don't know" just to make it stop, though she did know. At home that evening Sharmila, back from college for the weekend, watched her rehearse the next day's answer in the mirror, already pink. "Okay, three things," Sharmila said. "Breathe out slowly before you speak, longer out than in. Then look at something outside yourself, the blackboard or Mrs Sen's chalk, not at your own face in your head. And honestly? Most people are busy thinking about their own answers. They barely notice." Trisha rolled her eyes but tried it. Next morning, when her name came, she breathed out, fixed her eyes on the chalk and gave the answer. Her cheeks still warmed. But the boy beside her was busy drawing a cricket bat, and nobody said a word.

qa.q: What did Trisha whisper last week?
qa.a: Trisha whispered "I don't know", though she did know.

qa.q: What was Trisha afraid of when her name was called?
qa.a: Trisha was anxious about being seen blushing, sure the whole class could see the heat on her neck; it may also have been fear of getting the answer wrong.

qa.q: Which of Sharmila's steps helped, and how?
qa.a: Breathing out slowly, fixing her eyes on the chalk and remembering others are busy with their own answers eased the distress enough for Trisha to answer.

qa.q: How did the classmates react when Trisha answered?
qa.a: They barely noticed; the boy beside her was busy drawing a cricket bat, and nobody said a word.

grounding: It shows a teenager who blushes easily fearing being noticed, and slow breathing, outward focus and remembering others rarely notice reducing the distress.
